sections.heading: Model tier
sections.text: Materiality is scored High, the highest criterion score being the provision impact (loss allowance of EUR 96.2 million, 11.7% of the Bank's total loss allowance), with exposure Medium, own funds impact Low, customer impact Low and regulatory impact High. Complexity is scored Medium, driven by the multi-component methodology with scenario conditioning and by the dependencies on the IRB behavioural score and the scenario models. The materiality-by-complexity matrix of MRM-STD-010 §6.4 yields Tier 1, which is not lower than the minimum of Tier 2 for models used for financial reporting and meets FIN-STD-200 §4.5, which requires Tier 1 for ECL models covering more than 10% of the Bank loss allowance. As a Tier 1 model the model is approved by the Model Risk Committee, validated annually and monitored quarterly, and the materiality and complexity scores are recorded in the tiering template TT-MDL07-2027.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: ECL is measured with a PD/LGD/EAD approach at loan-part level in monthly time steps: for each scenario s, ECL_s = Σ_t PD_marg(t|s) × LGD(t|s) × EAD(t) × DF(t), and the reported ECL is the probability-weighted sum over the scenarios. The PD/LGD/EAD method was selected for this portfolio because 15 years of loan-level default, prepayment and collateral data are available and because collateral values, which drive mortgage losses, can be projected explicitly per scenario, whereas the loss-rate approach assessed in section 4.1 cannot. The components are: the staging module (section 4.2), the PD module with the 12-month hazard model and lifetime term structure (4.3), the prepayment module (4.3.2), the LGD module (4.4), the EAD module (4.5), the scenario module (4.6) and the ECL aggregation in the ECL engine (4.7); overlays are applied outside the model and documented in the management overlay memo EVD-07-OVL. For Stage 1 loan parts the 12-month ECL is the lifetime cash shortfall arising from defaults in the 12 months after the reporting date weighted by the probability of those defaults, i.e. the sum of the first 12 monthly terms of the formula above, and not the cash shortfall expected in the next 12 months.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text: The PD and prepayment modules are single models for the whole portfolio in which segment characteristics enter as drivers, because separate segment models would leave too few defaults in the NHG and interest-only segments. LGD pools are defined by NHG status, indexed LTV band (six bands) and, for Stage 3, time in default; prepayment pools by product type (annuity, linear, interest-only and savings- or investment-linked), remaining fixed-rate period and penalty-free headroom. These groupings share credit risk characteristics and are granular enough to assess changes in credit risk, and because staging is performed per loan part on the obligor's own lifetime PD, the performance of a pool cannot obscure an increase in credit risk of individual exposures. Segment-level performance is reported in section 7.2 and monitored per segment in chapter 10.

sections.text: The PD module uses the behavioural score of the IRB rating system PD-MORT-NL (currently version 3; the replacement by version 4, model MDL-01 in development, will be assessed as a change under MRM-STD-050), but only as a rank-ordering driver; the IRB PD with its long-run calibration, margin of conservatism and floors is not used, so no IRB adjustments need to be removed. In line with paragraph 75 of EBA/GL/2017/06, the model shares the Risk Data Hub, the definition of default, the collateral data and the scenario store with the IRB rating system, credit risk management and the ICAAP. Other dependencies are the macroeconomic scenarios and regional house price paths from the Enterprise Stress Testing scenario models (ERM-STD-300), the AVM indexation of the external provider, the Default Register and the forbearance and watchlist processes of Credit Risk Management. Changes in any of these inputs are notified to the model owner under the data change process described in section 4.1.1 of the RDS documentation.

sections.heading: Stage allocation
sections.text: At each monthly reporting date every loan part is allocated to Stage 3 if the obligor is in default under CR-STD-110, otherwise to Stage 2 if any Stage 2 criterion of section 4.2 is met, and otherwise to Stage 1; Stage 1 carries 12-month ECL, and Stages 2 and 3 carry lifetime ECL. The allocation is symmetrical: a loan part returns to Stage 1 and 12-month ECL as soon as no Stage 2 criterion is met at the reporting date, without probation other than the forborne-performing period, and leaves Stage 3 only after completion of the probation period of CR-STD-110. Because the quantitative criterion uses the probability-weighted forward-looking lifetime PD and is complemented by backstops and collective transfers, lifetime ECL is recognised for all loan parts with a significant increase in credit risk, whether identified individually or collectively. At 31 December 2026 Stage 1 comprises 418,950 loan parts with EUR 59.62 billion (92.0%), Stage 2 28,070 loan parts with EUR 4.64 billion (7.2%) and Stage 3 4,280 loan parts with EUR 0.54 billion (0.8%), with modelled ECL of EUR 8.9 million, EUR 27.6 million and EUR 41.3 million respectively.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives and selection
sections.text: For version 3.0 three methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation constraints): (A) a loss-rate approach with arrears roll rates; (B) TTC-to-PIT conversion of the IRB PD with a single systematic factor and a static lifetime curve; and (C) a discrete-time hazard model for default with a competing prepayment hazard and macroeconomic conditioning. Approach C was selected: it achieved an out-of-time Gini of 0.81 against 0.74 for approach B, models prepayment explicitly and produces scenario-conditioned lifetime term structures, while approach A cannot project lifetime losses with scenario-specific house prices and approach B inherits the long-run calibration of the IRB PD and underestimated the arrears after the 2022–2023 rate increase. Approach C is also the most transparent of the three (a logistic hazard with nine interpretable drivers), so the selection does not trade transparency for performance. Version 3.2 retains the methodology and re-estimates the coefficients and recalibrates the model on the 2026 RDS, so no new assessment of alternatives was required.

sections.heading: SICR – quantitative criterion
sections.text: At each reporting date the SICR test compares the annualised remaining-lifetime PD at the reporting date with the annualised lifetime PD that was expected at initial recognition for the same remaining term, both probability-weighted over the three scenarios, so that the assessment is based on the change in the risk of default over the expected life on a consistent remaining-life basis. The origination lifetime PD curve is stored per loan part at initial recognition (for loans originated before 2018 see section 4.2.5) and retained for the life of the loan part. A significant increase in credit risk is identified when the ratio of current to origination annualised lifetime PD exceeds 2.25 and the absolute increase in annualised lifetime PD exceeds 0.30 percentage points. The relative threshold makes a given absolute increase more significant for loans originated with a lower default risk, and the absolute threshold prevents transfers of low-PD loans on immaterial movements. The test uses the risk of default before the effect of collateral and NHG, which enter only the LGD, and not the change in expected credit losses.

sections.heading: SICR – backstops and qualitative indicators
sections.text: Irrespective of the quantitative criterion, a performing loan part is allocated to Stage 2 when the obligor is more than 30 days past due on an amount exceeding the EUR 100 and 1% threshold, when a forbearance measure has been granted, for at least the two-year forborne-performing probation period, or when the obligor is on the Intensive Care watchlist. The 30-days-past-due presumption serves as a backstop only: in 2026, 91% of loan parts that reached 30 days past due had already been transferred to Stage 2 earlier by the PD criterion or the watchlist, so past-due information is not the primary transfer indicator. The presumption is not rebutted for any part of the portfolio, and no dispensation to rebut it exists. The assessment is holistic and multifactor: the PD reflects behavioural scores, arrears history, changes in indexed LTV and payment shocks at interest rate resets, the backstops add forbearance and watchlist information, and the collective transfers of section 4.2.4 add forecast adverse conditions for specific groups, so that the indicators of IFRS 9 paragraph B5.5.17 relevant to mortgages are considered with a weight reflecting their relevance. Early-warning indicators of the portfolio (failed direct debits, BKR registrations, payment shock at rate reset and reported loss of income) trigger an Intensive Care review within 30 days, and obligors with confirmed deterioration are placed on the watchlist. The criteria are designed to transfer loan parts well before default: in 2026, 71% of defaulted loan parts had been in Stage 2 at least six months before default, so SICR recognition is not aligned with the point of default.

sections.heading: SICR – threshold calibration
sections.text: The relative and absolute thresholds were calibrated for the portfolio on reference dates 2019–2025 on the trade-off between the capture rate, being the share of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default, and stage volatility, being the share of loan parts moving between Stage 1 and Stage 2 more than twice within 12 months. The grid covered relative thresholds of 1.75, 2.0, 2.25, 2.5 and 3.0 and absolute thresholds of 0.20, 0.30 and 0.50 percentage points; the combination 2.0/0.20 gives a capture rate of 76% with volatility of 16.4%, 3.0/0.50 a capture rate of 58% with volatility of 5.1%, and the selected 2.25/0.30 a capture rate of 71% with volatility of 9.8% and a Stage 2 share of 7.2%. 'Significant' is thus defined by the portfolio's capture and stability trade-off and not by statistical significance, and the quantitative test is complemented by the qualitative backstops. The thresholds are re-assessed at least annually; the re-assessment for version 3.2 on data to December 2026 confirmed 2.25 and 0.30 percentage points.

sections.heading: SICR – collective assessment
sections.text: Where information indicating a significant increase in credit risk is available for a group but not yet reflected at loan-part level, SICR is assessed collectively in accordance with FIN-STD-200 §5.6. One collective transfer is in place: interest-only loan parts maturing in 2027–2034 whose obligors have an indexed LTV above 80% or an estimated refinancing capacity shortfall, in total 5,340 loan parts with EUR 1.21 billion, identified from the loan data and transferred to Stage 2 with population, triggering evidence and a quarterly review date recorded. This transfer corresponds to overlay OVL-M-01, so that the stage allocation is consistent with the measurement of the overlay. The need for further collective transfers is reviewed quarterly by IFRS 9 Modelling and Credit Risk Management on the basis of regional unemployment, sector information on large local employers and arrears trends.

sections.heading: Low credit risk, legacy origination PD and modified assets
sections.text: The low credit risk exemption is not applied: FIN-STD-200 §5.7 restricts it to debt securities with an investment-grade-equivalent internal rating, so every mortgage loan part is subject to the SICR test. For loan parts originated before 1 January 2018 (38% of the balance) the origination lifetime PD is a proxy obtained by applying the PD model to the origination characteristics and the macroeconomic conditions of the origination quarter; on 2018–2019 originations, for which both are available, stage allocation agrees for 97.8% of loan parts and the proxy increases the Stage 2 share by 0.3 percentage points. For modifications that do not lead to derecognition, such as interest rate resets and forbearance measures, SICR is assessed by comparing the lifetime PD at the reporting date based on the modified terms with the origination lifetime PD based on the original, unmodified terms. Modified loan parts are not treated as lower risk automatically: forborne loan parts remain in Stage 2 for at least the two-year probation, and return requires timely payments against the modified terms over that period.

sections.heading: PD – 12-month hazard model and variable selection
sections.text: The monthly default hazard is modelled by logistic regression on obligor-months; the 61 candidate variables were assessed for economic rationale, availability at the reporting date in production and stability over time (annual PSI below 0.10). Selection proceeded by univariate analysis (Gini and monotonicity), clustering of correlated variables with an absolute correlation above 0.6, keeping the strongest per cluster, and stepwise multivariate selection at a 1% significance level with business review; the nine final drivers all have the expected sign: behavioural score (negative), maximum arrears in the last 12 months (positive), indexed LTV (positive), payment shock at rate reset (positive), NHG (negative), loan-to-income at origination (positive), seasoning (spline), change in unemployment (positive) and change in house prices (negative). No protected attribute was a candidate variable, and the postcode was excluded from the candidate set following the proxy screening in section 7.5 of the RDS documentation. From 14 macroeconomic candidates, the year-on-year change in the unemployment rate (lag two quarters, coefficient 0.21 per percentage point, p < 0.001) and the year-on-year change in the house price index (lag one quarter, coefficient −0.018 per percentage point, p < 0.001) were retained; GDP growth was rejected for collinearity with unemployment and a wrong sign in the multivariate model, and the mortgage rate because it is captured by the loan-level payment shock. Out of sample on 2024–2025, the macro-conditioned model reduced the absolute error of the predicted annual default rate from 0.08 to 0.03 percentage points compared with the model without macro terms.

sections.heading: PD – lifetime term structure and prepayment
sections.text: The monthly default hazard h_d and prepayment hazard h_p are chained into a lifetime term structure with survival S(t) = Π(1 − h_d(k) − h_p(k)) and marginal PD(t) = S(t−1) × h_d(t), over the remaining contractual maturity of each loan part, which gives a point-in-time PD term structure over the expected life of each exposure. The prepayment hazard comes from a multinomial logit model for full redemption and partial prepayment with drivers refinancing incentive, remaining fixed-rate period, penalty-free headroom, seasoning and regional housing turnover, estimated on 2015–2026, which reflects expected prepayments in the measurement; the baseline annual prepayment rate for 2027 is 5.8% against 5.4% observed in 2026. The macroeconomic drivers are applied over the reasonable and supportable forecast period of three years (2027–2029); in 2030–2031 they revert linearly to their long-run averages over two years, after which hazards correspond to the long-run default rate of 0.63%, so that ECL for exposures with lives beyond the forecast horizon is estimated by a documented process. By construction of the survival formulation cumulative PD curves are monotonically non-decreasing and marginal PDs are non-negative, and the ECL engine verifies both conditions per loan part at each run.

sections.heading: LGD
sections.text: For performing loan parts LGD = P(cure) × LGD_cure + (1 − P(cure)) × LGL; P(cure) is a logistic model with drivers indexed LTV, NHG, arrears amount and, for Stage 3, time in default (average 63%), and LGD_cure is 1.2% (costs and interest loss). The loss given liquidation is the shortfall of the exposure over the collateral proceeds, being the indexed property value projected with the scenario house price path, less a forced-sale discount of 12.5%, sale costs of 3.0% plus EUR 4,500, discounted over a time to sale of 16 months, and for NHG loan parts the guarantee payment with a claim acceptance rate of 94%; foreclosure proceeds are included whether or not foreclosure is probable. Collateral values are indexed from the latest valuation to the reporting date and projected with the scenario-specific regional (COROP) house price paths of each macroeconomic scenario. The LGD is a best estimate without downturn adjustment, margin of conservatism or regulatory LGD floors, and recoveries and directly attributable costs are discounted at the effective interest rate of the loan part. Loan parts are written off when the property has been sold and there is no reasonable expectation of recovering the residual debt; recoveries after write-off (on average 6% of the residual debt) are included in realised LGD, consistent with this write-off policy. The average LGD of performing loan parts is 7.4% in the baseline scenario, 5.8% in the upside and 12.9% in the downside scenario.

sections.heading: EAD and expected life
sections.text: The EAD term structure follows the contractual repayment schedule per loan part and repayment type, reduced by expected partial prepayments and including accrued interest; binding offers are converted with a credit conversion factor of 78%, estimated on the drawdown of offers within their validity period in 2019–2026. The expected life equals the remaining contractual maturity (on average 21.6 years, maximum 30 years), and the ECL horizon never exceeds the maximum contractual period over which the Bank is exposed to credit risk. The portfolio contains no revolving facilities, so the behavioural measurement period of IFRS 9 paragraph 5.5.20 and FIN-STD-200 §8.3 does not apply. Prepayment is accounted for consistently in the lifetime PD (as competing risk) and in the EAD (as balance reduction), using the same prepayment module.

sections.heading: Forward-looking information – scenarios and weights
sections.text: ECL is computed under the baseline, upside and downside scenarios produced by Enterprise Stress Testing under ERM-STD-300; the baseline equals the scenario of the financial plan 2027–2029 approved by the Management Board on 8 December 2026, so that forward-looking information is consistent with budgets and capital planning. The Q4 2026 baseline assumes Dutch GDP growth of 1.3%, 1.5% and 1.6% in 2027–2029, unemployment of 3.9–4.1% and house price growth of 4.5%, 3.0% and 2.5%; the downside assumes a GDP contraction of 1.8% in 2027, unemployment peaking at 6.4% in 2028 and a cumulative house price fall of 15% over 2027–2028; the upside assumes GDP growth of 2.4%, unemployment of 3.5% and house price growth of 7.0% in 2027.

sections.heading: ECL calculation, discounting and modifications
sections.text: Expected cash shortfalls are discounted to the reporting date, not to the expected default date, using the effective interest rate of the loan part determined at initial recognition; for variable-rate loan parts (3.4% of the balance) the current effective interest rate is used. The resulting estimate is unbiased and probability-weighted, reflects a range of outcomes and the time value of money and uses reasonable and supportable information available without undue cost or effort, and contains no margins of conservatism, downturn components or regulatory floors. The ECL engine calculates the monthly terms per loan part and scenario up to the remaining maturity, aggregates them to 12-month ECL (first 12 months) and lifetime ECL, and applies the stage from the staging module. Results are reported per loan part to the finance subledger and aggregated by stage, product, NHG status and LTV band for management reporting. For modifications that do not result in derecognition, Finance recalculates the gross carrying amount as the present value of the modified contractual cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate and recognises a modification gain or loss in profit or loss, and the ECL engine uses the recalculated gross carrying amount. A modification leads to derecognition when the present value of the modified cash flows differs by more than 10% from that of the original cash flows or on qualitative grounds such as a change of borrower; a new loan recognised after derecognition of a credit-impaired loan is identified as POCI. Interest rate resets at the end of a fixed-rate period are contractual repricings and not modifications. In 2026, 1,840 forbearance measures were granted, with modification losses of EUR 0.9 million.

sections.heading: Stage 3 and purchased or originated credit-impaired assets
sections.text: Stage 3 comprises the loan parts of obligors in default under CR-STD-110, whose triggers capture the observable events of the IFRS 9 definition of a credit-impaired asset, namely significant financial difficulty of the borrower, a breach of contract such as more than 90 days past due, distressed concessions and probable bankruptcy, including the combined effect of several events through the case-by-case UTP assessment. For Stage 3 obligors with a total exposure of EUR 1 million or more (23 obligors, EUR 31 million), the workout function measures ECL individually as the difference between the gross carrying amount and the present value of probability-weighted estimated cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate; all other Stage 3 loan parts use the LGD module with time-in-default dependent LGD. Fourteen loan parts (EUR 3.1 million) are purchased or originated credit-impaired, arising from the derecognition of forborne loans; for these the allowance equals only the cumulative change in lifetime ECL since initial recognition, without staging.

sections.heading: Reconciliation with IRB definitions and parameters
sections.text: Key terms are defined consistently with credit risk management and the IRB approach: default follows CR-STD-110, loss is the economic loss including directly attributable costs, and cure follows the exit from default; the differences with the IRB parameters (point-in-time instead of long-run and downturn calibration, discounting at the effective interest rate instead of the IRB discount rate, lifetime instead of 12-month horizon) and their rationale were approved by the Group Impairment Committee on 17 October 2024 as part of the approval of version 3.0. The IRB LGD model for residential mortgages is not reused; applying its downturn LGD including margin of conservatism would raise the average performing LGD from 7.4% to 14.8% and the modelled ECL at 31 December 2026 by EUR 41 million, which quantifies the effect of the IFRS 9-specific design choices. Both models use the same cure definition and the same forced-sale data, so that differences between the two parameters are limited to the framework-driven design choices listed above.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: The intercept of the hazard model is calibrated so that the predicted 12-month default rate over 2024–2026 equals the observed default rate of 0.40% adjusted to current conditions through the macroeconomic terms; the long-run average default rate is not used as the calibration target. After calibration the predicted 12-month default rate for 2026 is 0.43% against an observed 0.41%. For performance testing and monitoring, loan parts are grouped into ten PD bands (P01–P10, from below 0.05% to above 5%), which are not used for staging or measurement. The prepayment model is calibrated to the observed 2024–2026 prepayment rates, and the cure model and the forced-sale discount to 2022–2026 workouts and sales, while the loss given liquidation parameters are reviewed annually against the most recent sales.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: Not applicable: IFRS 9 requires unbiased estimates, and FIN-STD-200 §4.1 excludes margins of conservatism from ECL risk parameters. Identified model limitations that could bias the estimate are addressed through recalibration or, as an interim solution, through overlays under chapter 11, not through a margin of conservatism. The data deficiencies of the RDS documentation are treated as described in its section 6.2 and in the limitations log in chapter 8.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power and stability
sections.text: Discriminatory power of the 12-month hazard model was tested on the development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples with thresholds consistent with MV-HB-003: the Gini coefficient is 0.83 on development, 0.82 on out-of-sample and 0.81 on out-of-time data (95% DeLong interval 0.79–0.83), well above the red threshold of 0.50 for retail behavioural PD. The Gini of the previous model version 3.1 on the same out-of-time sample is 0.80. The ordering of default rates across the ten PD bands is monotonic on all three samples. Stability was tested by the PSI of the score and drivers between the development sample and the out-of-time sample (score 0.05, drivers 0.01–0.11) and by re-estimating the model on rolling five-year windows, in which all coefficients keep their sign and remain within two standard errors of the full-sample estimate. The stage distribution was stable over the last eight quarters, with a Stage 2 share between 6.8% and 7.6% of exposure. The prepayment model is stable except for 2022, when the refinancing incentive turned negative; the model captures this through the incentive driver.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and performance by segment
sections.text: Calibration accuracy was tested on the out-of-time sample with the Jeffreys test applied two-sided, as required for unbiased IFRS 9 estimates: at portfolio level the predicted default rate (0.44%) is not significantly different from the observed rate (0.42%, p = 0.41), and per PD band nine bands are green and band P07 shows significant overestimation (p = 0.03, amber). The overestimation in P07 was analysed and attributed to loans with a payment shock indicator whose rate reset occurred at lower market rates than assumed, and is recorded in the limitations log as L-09 with recalibration of the payment shock variable planned for version 4.0. Performance was tested for the whole model and for each material segment (NHG and non-NHG, annuity, linear, interest-only and savings-linked products, LTV bands and PD bands): Gini ranges from 0.74 (interest-only) to 0.84 (annuity). The only metric outside its threshold is the calibration of the interest-only segment on the out-of-time sample (observed 0.52% against predicted 0.44%, amber), analysed as caused by refinancing risk at maturity that is not captured by the drivers, recorded as limitation L-01 and addressed by overlay OVL-M-01 and the planned model change to version 4.0. The LGD model performs within tolerance for NHG and non-NHG loans (section 7.7).

sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger model
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model, the model is compared with a challenger model, the TTC-to-PIT conversion of the IRB PD (approach B of section 4.1), which is run quarterly in parallel. On the out-of-time sample the challenger has a Gini of 0.74 against 0.81 and a larger calibration error (0.11 against 0.02 percentage points), and at 31 December 2026 it produces a modelled ECL of EUR 82.4 million against EUR 77.8 million; the difference is explained by the higher lifetime PDs of the challenger for seasoned annuity loans, whose static lifetime curve does not reflect their amortisation, so the challenger does not outperform the model on any material metric. The ECL coverage ratio of 15 basis points is within the range of 9–18 basis points disclosed by four other Dutch mortgage lenders for 2026, which serves as an external benchmark.

sections.heading: Back-testing of staging, PD, LGD and CCF
sections.text: Back-testing is performed annually: the 12-month PIT PD per PD band against observed default rates (section 7.2), LGD on closed workouts, the conversion factor of binding offers, and the stage allocation, including the share of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default and the frequency of stage reversals. For 2026 the share of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default is 71% (2025: 68%), stage reversals from Stage 2 to Stage 1 within three months affect 11.4% of transfers, the predicted LGD on 2025–2026 closed workouts is 9.6% against a realised 8.9%, and the predicted conversion of offers is 78% against 81% observed. Internally established performance standards are defined for each back-testing metric in chapter 10, and a significant breach leads to remedial action up to recalibration or redevelopment.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: All material assumptions on data, driver–target relationships, their stability and the intended use have been identified and assessed for plausibility: (A1) the relationship between defaults, prepayments and macroeconomic conditions observed in 2012–2026 continues to hold; (A2) regional house price paths from the scenario models are unbiased; (A3) the forced-sale discount and sale costs remain stable; (A4) mortgages are not extended beyond their contractual maturity; (A5) NHG claims are honoured at the observed acceptance rate; (A6) the proxy origination PD for pre-2018 loans is representative. A1 and A2 are supported by the out-of-time and macro back-testing results, A3 and A5 are reviewed annually against realised sales and claims, A4 follows from the contractual terms and A6 is supported by the comparison in section 4.2.5. The assumptions are reviewed at each annual model review.

sections.heading: Limitations log
sections.text: The limitations log of the model is complete in this chapter; each entry states an identifier, description, source, estimated impact, mitigating measure and owner. L-01: refinancing risk of interest-only loans at maturity not captured by the PD drivers; source: segment calibration (section 7.2); impact EUR 14.6 million; mitigation overlay OVL-M-01, collective Stage 2 transfer and version 4.0; owner M. Hoekstra. L-02: physical climate risk from foundation subsidence in peat areas not captured by collateral indexation; impact EUR 3.8 million; mitigation overlay OVL-M-02; owner M. Hoekstra. L-03: approximated default flag 2012–2015 (DD-01); impact limited to long-run reversion level (±EUR 0.4 million); mitigation PIT calibration on 2024–2026; owner L. Verbeek. L-04: proxy origination PD for pre-2018 loans; impact +0.3 percentage points Stage 2 share; owner L. Verbeek. L-05: imputed original valuations (DD-03); impact below 0.5% of PD; remediation at source. L-06: single national unemployment driver; impact not quantified, assessed medium; owner L. Verbeek. L-07: watchlist history from 2019 only (DD-04). L-08: prepayment reason codes before 2015 (DD-05). L-09: overestimation in PD band P07 (section 7.2).

sections.heading: Implementation specification and handover
sections.text: The handover to implementation consists of implementation specification IS-MDL07-v3.2, approved by the model owner on 23 April 2027, the parameter table PARAM_ECL_MORT_V32 with all coefficients, lookup tables and pool definitions, 1,200 test cases with expected outputs produced with the development code, and reference ECL outputs for 31 December 2026 from the development environment. The specification defines every transformation, missing-value and outlier treatment, formula, coefficient and lookup table with precision and rounding conventions, and its test cases cover typical cases, boundary values, missing and invalid inputs and every segment, stage and PD band. The production ECL engine is operated by Finance IT; model developers have no write access to its production environment. Implementation testing, record-level reconciliation, the parallel run and user acceptance testing for version 3.2 are documented in the implementation and parallel run report EVD-07-IMPL.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan
sections.text: The monitoring plan of the model is documented in this chapter; it was approved by the model owner before go-live of version 3.0 and reviewed by Model Validation in 2024. For each KPI the plan defines the calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference periods, segments, responsible person and escalation per traffic light; monitoring is performed quarterly, as required for a Tier 1 model, by IFRS 9 Modelling. The KPIs cover discriminatory power, calibration of PD, LGD and conversion factors, population and characteristic stability, production data quality, stage overrides and overlays, staging performance and model coverage, and are computed for the whole portfolio and per segment and PD band.

sections.heading: KPIs and thresholds
sections.text: Population stability: PSI of the score and of each input variable against the development sample, green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25. Discrimination: Gini on the latest 12-month window compared with development, amber at a relative decline above 10% and red above 20%, and red in any case below 0.50 for this retail model. PD calibration: realised default rates against PD per band and for the portfolio with the Jeffreys test of MV-HB-003, applied two-sided for this IFRS 9 model, amber at p < 5% and red at p < 1%. LGD and conversion factor: realised against estimated values per pool and for the portfolio, amber when the portfolio underestimation exceeds 5% relative and red above 10%. Staging: share of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default, amber below 60% and red below 50%; overlays in place with amount, purpose and planned removal date; model coverage, being the share of in-scope loan parts with a model ECL, and loan parts with missing or outdated inputs.

sections.heading: Reporting, escalation and annual review
sections.text: Monitoring results are reported to the model owner, Model Risk Management, Model Validation and Credit Risk Management. Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive quarters, is notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, followed within 60 calendar days by a root cause analysis and an action plan proposing no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use. In line with FIN-STD-200 §12.3 a red outcome leads to an MRC-approved remediation plan within three months and an assessment of the need for a temporary overlay. The annual model review by the model owner covers monitoring results, portfolio and environment changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and overlays, and code-documentation consistency, and concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose; it is signed off by the model owner and submitted to MRM (for 2026: report EVD-07-MON).

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: Every expert judgement applied in the development and application of the model is recorded in the expert judgement log EJL-MDL-07, stored with the model documentation, with its type, lifecycle stage and affected data, segment or parameter; judgements in data treatment are also referenced in the RDS documentation. Each entry records the rationale, the evidence relied on and the alternatives considered and rejected, and the quantified impact on the ECL or the reason why quantification is not possible. The log contains eight active entries: EJ-RDS-01 (COVID-19 payment holiday treatment), EJ-RDS-02 (product code mapping), EJ-MDD-01 (single PD model with segment drivers), EJ-MDD-02 (two-year reversion period), EJ-MDD-03 (rejection of GDP as driver), EJ-MDD-04 (NHG claim acceptance rate), EJ-MDD-05 (forced-sale discount floor of 10%) and EJ-OVL-01 (quantification of overlay OVL-M-01); each is described in this chapter or in the overlay memo with its log reference.

sections.heading: Materiality, approval and challenge of expert judgement; stage overrides
sections.text: Each judgement is classified by its impact on the ECL relative to the output without the judgement or the best statistical alternative: EJ-OVL-01 is high (15% of the allowance), EJ-MDD-02, EJ-MDD-04 and EJ-MDD-05 are medium, and the others low. Approval follows materiality: low judgements by the model owner, medium by the model owner and the head of the modelling unit, high by the MRC after review by Model Validation; the proposer is never the sole approver. Medium and high judgements were challenged by Daan Kuipers, who did not propose them, before approval, and the challenge and its resolution are recorded in the log, for example the challenge of EJ-MDD-05, which led to lowering the floor from 12.5% to 10%. The aggregate effect of all expert judgements, including the overlays, is EUR 20.1 million or 21% of the allowance, which exceeds the high materiality threshold and was approved by the MRC on 18 March 2027. Manual stage overrides are permitted only within the override policy in section 6 of the ECL operating procedure OP-ECL-04, which lists the permitted reasons in a closed list (information on imminent unemployment or divorce not yet reflected in the data, confirmed fraud investigation, and errors in input data pending correction), limits overrides to an upward transfer to Stage 2, and requires relevant information not captured by the model. Each override records the reason code, a written rationale with supporting evidence, the proposer from Collections and the approver from Credit Risk Management, independent of the proposer. Override rates, direction and magnitude are monitored quarterly by reason and approving unit; the rate was 0.4% of loan parts in 2026, below the retail analysis threshold of 5%.

sections.heading: Expert judgement in model design
sections.text: The design judgements are justified in this document: the single PD model with segment drivers instead of segment models (EJ-MDD-01, section 2.2), the two-year reversion period at the upper end of FIN-STD-200 §9.4 (EJ-MDD-02, section 4.3.2), the rejection of GDP as a driver (EJ-MDD-03, section 4.3.1), the NHG claim acceptance rate of 94% (EJ-MDD-04) and the floor of 10% on the forced-sale discount (EJ-MDD-05, section 4.4). EJ-MDD-04 uses the observed acceptance rate of 2016–2026 claims (1,212 claims) rather than the lower 2013–2015 rate, because the NHG conditions were tightened in 2014 and the Bank's claim handling was centralised in 2016. EJ-MDD-05 sets a floor because the observed discount fell to 8.1% in 2021–2022, when the housing market was exceptionally tight, which is not considered representative for the lifetime of the portfolio.

evidence.quote: The design judgements are justified in this document: the single PD model with segment drivers instead of segment models (EJ-MDD-01, section 2.2), the two-year reversion period at the upper end of FIN-STD-200 §9.4 (EJ-MDD-02, section 4.3.2), the rejection of GDP as a driver (EJ-MDD-03, section 4.3.1), the NHG claim acceptance rate of 94% (EJ-MDD-04) and the floor of 10% on the forced-sale discount (EJ-MDD-05, section 4.4).

sections.heading: Overlays
sections.text: Each overlay addresses a specific identified model limitation, is quantified by a documented method and has a plan with target date to remove the limitation: OVL-M-01 addresses L-01 and is to be removed by model version 4.0, and OVL-M-02 addresses L-02 and is to be removed when the climate-adjusted collateral indexation becomes available. Both overlays are recorded in the overlay register with rationale, limitation addressed, affected portfolio and stages, quantification method, amount, approval, review date and remediation plan, and are documented in the management overlay memo EVD-07-OVL. OVL-M-01 (EUR 14.6 million at 31 December 2026) exceeds EUR 5 million and was approved by the Group Impairment Committee after review by Model Validation; OVL-M-02 (EUR 3.8 million, 4% of the portfolio allowance) was approved jointly by the Head of IFRS 9 Modelling and the Head of Finance Reporting. Overlays are reassessed quarterly, and because OVL-M-01 had been in place for four consecutive quarters by 31 March 2026, a model change assessment under MRM-STD-050 was opened (CHG-2026-0118), which led to the planned development of version 4.0.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: ECL-MORT-NL measures the loss allowance for expected credit losses on all Dutch residential mortgage loans of the Bank and its mortgage label subsidiary measured at amortised cost, and on the related loan commitments (binding mortgage offers); the portfolio contains no financial guarantee contracts, lease receivables or assets at fair value through other comprehensive income. For loan commitments, the date on which the customer accepts the binding offer, which makes the Bank party to an irrevocable commitment, is the date of initial recognition for impairment purposes and the reference point for the SICR assessment; the origination PD curve is fixed at that date. The model produces the 12-month and lifetime ECL per loan part at each month-end, the stage allocation, and the scenario-specific ECL used for the IFRS 7 sensitivity disclosures; secondary uses are the cost-of-risk projections in the financial plan, the ICAAP and the EU-wide stress test. Main users are Finance Reporting, which books the allowance, Credit Risk Management, which uses the stage distribution and cost of risk in the credit risk appetite reporting, and Enterprise Stress Testing. The expected loss and cost-of-risk metrics of the mortgage portfolio in the credit risk appetite statement are measured with the output of this registered and approved model. The model output is not used in decisions on individual customers: the stage allocation and loan-part ECL do not enter acceptance, pricing, limit or collections decisions, also not through third parties, so that no automated individual decision with legal or similarly significant effects within the meaning of Article 22 GDPR arises. At 31 December 2026 the portfolio comprises 451,300 loan parts of 262,800 obligors with a gross carrying amount of EUR 64.8 billion and EUR 1.9 billion of binding offers, and the loss allowance amounts to EUR 96.2 million, of which EUR 77.8 million modelled and EUR 18.4 million overlays.

sections.heading: Model tier
sections.text: Materiality is scored High, the highest criterion score being the provision impact (loss allowance of EUR 96.2 million, 11.7% of the Bank's total loss allowance), with exposure Medium, own funds impact Low, customer impact Low and regulatory impact High. Complexity is scored Medium, driven by the multi-component methodology with scenario conditioning and by the dependencies on the IRB behavioural score and the scenario models. The materiality-by-complexity matrix of MRM-STD-010 §6.4 yields Tier 1, which is not lower than the minimum of Tier 2 for models used for financial reporting and meets FIN-STD-200 §4.5, which requires Tier 1 for ECL models covering more than 10% of the Bank loss allowance. As a Tier 1 model the model is approved by the Model Risk Committee, validated annually and monitored quarterly, and the materiality and complexity scores are recorded in the tiering template TT-MDL07-2027.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: ECL is measured with a PD/LGD/EAD approach at loan-part level in monthly time steps: for each scenario s, ECL_s = Σ_t PD_marg(t|s) × LGD(t|s) × EAD(t) × DF(t), and the reported ECL is the probability-weighted sum over the scenarios. The PD/LGD/EAD method was selected for this portfolio because 15 years of loan-level default, prepayment and collateral data are available and because collateral values, which drive mortgage losses, can be projected explicitly per scenario, whereas the loss-rate approach assessed in section 4.1 cannot. The components are: the staging module (section 4.2), the PD module with the 12-month hazard model and lifetime term structure (4.3), the prepayment module (4.3.2), the LGD module (4.4), the EAD module (4.5), the scenario module (4.6) and the ECL aggregation in the ECL engine (4.7); overlays are applied outside the model and documented in the management overlay memo EVD-07-OVL. For Stage 1 loan parts the 12-month ECL is the lifetime cash shortfall arising from defaults in the 12 months after the reporting date weighted by the probability of those defaults, i.e. the sum of the first 12 monthly terms of the formula above, and not the cash shortfall expected in the next 12 months.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text: The PD and prepayment modules are single models for the whole portfolio in which segment characteristics enter as drivers, because separate segment models would leave too few defaults in the NHG and interest-only segments. LGD pools are defined by NHG status, indexed LTV band (six bands) and, for Stage 3, time in default; prepayment pools by product type (annuity, linear, interest-only and savings- or investment-linked), remaining fixed-rate period and penalty-free headroom. These groupings share credit risk characteristics and are granular enough to assess changes in credit risk, and because staging is performed per loan part on the obligor's own lifetime PD, the performance of a pool cannot obscure an increase in credit risk of individual exposures. Segment-level performance is reported in section 7.2 and monitored per segment in chapter 10.

sections.text: The PD module uses the behavioural score of the IRB rating system PD-MORT-NL (currently version 3; the replacement by version 4, model MDL-01 in development, will be assessed as a change under MRM-STD-050), but only as a rank-ordering driver; the IRB PD with its long-run calibration, margin of conservatism and floors is not used, so no IRB adjustments need to be removed. In line with paragraph 75 of EBA/GL/2017/06, the model shares the Risk Data Hub, the definition of default, the collateral data and the scenario store with the IRB rating system, credit risk management and the ICAAP. Other dependencies are the macroeconomic scenarios and regional house price paths from the Enterprise Stress Testing scenario models (ERM-STD-300), the AVM indexation of the external provider, the Default Register and the forbearance and watchlist processes of Credit Risk Management. Changes in any of these inputs are notified to the model owner under the data change process described in section 4.1.1 of the RDS documentation.

sections.heading: Stage allocation
sections.text: At each monthly reporting date every loan part is allocated to Stage 3 if the obligor is in default under CR-STD-110, otherwise to Stage 2 if any Stage 2 criterion of section 4.2 is met, and otherwise to Stage 1; Stage 1 carries 12-month ECL, and Stages 2 and 3 carry lifetime ECL. The allocation is symmetrical: a loan part returns to Stage 1 and 12-month ECL as soon as no Stage 2 criterion is met at the reporting date, without probation other than the forborne-performing period, and leaves Stage 3 only after completion of the probation period of CR-STD-110. Because the quantitative criterion uses the probability-weighted forward-looking lifetime PD and is complemented by backstops and collective transfers, lifetime ECL is recognised for all loan parts with a significant increase in credit risk, whether identified individually or collectively. At 31 December 2026 Stage 1 comprises 418,950 loan parts with EUR 59.62 billion (92.0%), Stage 2 28,070 loan parts with EUR 4.64 billion (7.2%) and Stage 3 4,280 loan parts with EUR 0.54 billion (0.8%), with modelled ECL of EUR 8.9 million, EUR 27.6 million and EUR 41.3 million respectively.

sections.heading: Reference data set and samples
sections.text: The model is estimated and calibrated on the frozen RDS RDS-ECLM-2026-v1.0, documented in the approved RDS documentation EVD-07-RDS version 1.0; the same version identifier is recorded in chapter 12. The input data meet the internal data quality standards of MRM-STD-022: the data quality assessment EVD-07-DQ concluded that the historical, current and forward-looking data are relevant, accurate, reliable and complete, and the exclusions were shown not to bias the ECL estimate (RDS section 5.3). Data deficiencies DD-01 to DD-05 of the RDS documentation are cross-referenced to limitations L-03, L-05, L-07 and L-08 in chapter 8. Macroeconomic history and scenario paths for 2027–2031 are taken from the scenario store as of the Q4 2026 scenario approval. The samples were defined in the development plan before estimation: development sample of 70% of obligors on reference dates January 2014 – December 2023 (19.4 million obligor-months, 9,830 defaults), out-of-sample hold-out of the remaining 30% of obligors on the same dates (8.3 million obligor-months, 4,190 defaults) and out-of-time sample January 2024 – December 2025 (6.1 million obligor-months, 2,070 defaults). The out-of-time sample was used only for performance testing and not for variable selection or parameter estimation. The 12-month point-in-time calibration uses calendar years 2024–2026, including the out-of-time years, which is a calibration step after estimation and does not affect the out-of-time discrimination results. The LGD and prepayment samples are described in sections 4.3.2 and 4.4 and in the RDS documentation.

The input data meet the internal data quality standards of MRM-STD-022: the data quality assessment EVD-07-DQ concluded that the historical, current and forward-looking data are relevant, accurate, reliable and complete, and the exclusions were shown not to bias the ECL estimate (RDS section 5.3).

The samples were defined in the development plan before estimation: development sample of 70% of obligors on reference dates January 2014 – December 2023 (19.4 million obligor-months, 9,830 defaults), out-of-sample hold-out of the remaining 30% of obligors on the same dates (8.3 million obligor-months, 4,190 defaults) and out-of-time sample January 2024 – December 2025 (6.1 million obligor-months, 2,070 defaults).

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives and selection
sections.text: For version 3.0 three methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation constraints): (A) a loss-rate approach with arrears roll rates; (B) TTC-to-PIT conversion of the IRB PD with a single systematic factor and a static lifetime curve; and (C) a discrete-time hazard model for default with a competing prepayment hazard and macroeconomic conditioning. Approach C was selected: it achieved an out-of-time Gini of 0.81 against 0.74 for approach B, models prepayment explicitly and produces scenario-conditioned lifetime term structures, while approach A cannot project lifetime losses with scenario-specific house prices and approach B inherits the long-run calibration of the IRB PD and underestimated the arrears after the 2022–2023 rate increase. Approach C is also the most transparent of the three (a logistic hazard with nine interpretable drivers), so the selection does not trade transparency for performance. Version 3.2 retains the methodology and re-estimates the coefficients and recalibrates the model on the 2026 RDS, so no new assessment of alternatives was required.

sections.heading: SICR – quantitative criterion
sections.text: At each reporting date the SICR test compares the annualised remaining-lifetime PD at the reporting date with the annualised lifetime PD that was expected at initial recognition for the same remaining term, both probability-weighted over the three scenarios, so that the assessment is based on the change in the risk of default over the expected life on a consistent remaining-life basis. The origination lifetime PD curve is stored per loan part at initial recognition (for loans originated before 2018 see section 4.2.5) and retained for the life of the loan part. A significant increase in credit risk is identified when the ratio of current to origination annualised lifetime PD exceeds 2.25 and the absolute increase in annualised lifetime PD exceeds 0.30 percentage points. The relative threshold makes a given absolute increase more significant for loans originated with a lower default risk, and the absolute threshold prevents transfers of low-PD loans on immaterial movements. The test uses the risk of default before the effect of collateral and NHG, which enter only the LGD, and not the change in expected credit losses.

sections.heading: SICR – backstops and qualitative indicators
sections.text: Irrespective of the quantitative criterion, a performing loan part is allocated to Stage 2 when the obligor is more than 30 days past due on an amount exceeding the EUR 100 and 1% threshold, when a forbearance measure has been granted, for at least the two-year forborne-performing probation period, or when the obligor is on the Intensive Care watchlist. The 30-days-past-due presumption serves as a backstop only: in 2026, 91% of loan parts that reached 30 days past due had already been transferred to Stage 2 earlier by the PD criterion or the watchlist, so past-due information is not the primary transfer indicator. The presumption is not rebutted for any part of the portfolio, and no dispensation to rebut it exists. The assessment is holistic and multifactor: the PD reflects behavioural scores, arrears history, changes in indexed LTV and payment shocks at interest rate resets, the backstops add forbearance and watchlist information, and the collective transfers of section 4.2.4 add forecast adverse conditions for specific groups, so that the indicators of IFRS 9 paragraph B5.5.17 relevant to mortgages are considered with a weight reflecting their relevance. Early-warning indicators of the portfolio (failed direct debits, BKR registrations, payment shock at rate reset and reported loss of income) trigger an Intensive Care review within 30 days, and obligors with confirmed deterioration are placed on the watchlist. The criteria are designed to transfer loan parts well before default: in 2026, 71% of defaulted loan parts had been in Stage 2 at least six months before default, so SICR recognition is not aligned with the point of default.

sections.heading: SICR – threshold calibration
sections.text: The relative and absolute thresholds were calibrated for the portfolio on reference dates 2019–2025 on the trade-off between the capture rate, being the share of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default, and stage volatility, being the share of loan parts moving between Stage 1 and Stage 2 more than twice within 12 months. The grid covered relative thresholds of 1.75, 2.0, 2.25, 2.5 and 3.0 and absolute thresholds of 0.20, 0.30 and 0.50 percentage points; the combination 2.0/0.20 gives a capture rate of 76% with volatility of 16.4%, 3.0/0.50 a capture rate of 58% with volatility of 5.1%, and the selected 2.25/0.30 a capture rate of 71% with volatility of 9.8% and a Stage 2 share of 7.2%. 'Significant' is thus defined by the portfolio's capture and stability trade-off and not by statistical significance, and the quantitative test is complemented by the qualitative backstops. The thresholds are re-assessed at least annually; the re-assessment for version 3.2 on data to December 2026 confirmed 2.25 and 0.30 percentage points.

sections.heading: SICR – collective assessment
sections.text: Where information indicating a significant increase in credit risk is available for a group but not yet reflected at loan-part level, SICR is assessed collectively in accordance with FIN-STD-200 §5.6. One collective transfer is in place: interest-only loan parts maturing in 2027–2034 whose obligors have an indexed LTV above 80% or an estimated refinancing capacity shortfall, in total 5,340 loan parts with EUR 1.21 billion, identified from the loan data and transferred to Stage 2 with population, triggering evidence and a quarterly review date recorded. This transfer corresponds to overlay OVL-M-01, so that the stage allocation is consistent with the measurement of the overlay. The need for further collective transfers is reviewed quarterly by IFRS 9 Modelling and Credit Risk Management on the basis of regional unemployment, sector information on large local employers and arrears trends.

sections.heading: Low credit risk, legacy origination PD and modified assets
sections.text: The low credit risk exemption is not applied: FIN-STD-200 §5.7 restricts it to debt securities with an investment-grade-equivalent internal rating, so every mortgage loan part is subject to the SICR test. For loan parts originated before 1 January 2018 (38% of the balance) the origination lifetime PD is a proxy obtained by applying the PD model to the origination characteristics and the macroeconomic conditions of the origination quarter; on 2018–2019 originations, for which both are available, stage allocation agrees for 97.8% of loan parts and the proxy increases the Stage 2 share by 0.3 percentage points. For modifications that do not lead to derecognition, such as interest rate resets and forbearance measures, SICR is assessed by comparing the lifetime PD at the reporting date based on the modified terms with the origination lifetime PD based on the original, unmodified terms. Modified loan parts are not treated as lower risk automatically: forborne loan parts remain in Stage 2 for at least the two-year probation, and return requires timely payments against the modified terms over that period.

sections.heading: PD – 12-month hazard model and variable selection
sections.text: The monthly default hazard is modelled by logistic regression on obligor-months; the 61 candidate variables were assessed for economic rationale, availability at the reporting date in production and stability over time (annual PSI below 0.10). Selection proceeded by univariate analysis (Gini and monotonicity), clustering of correlated variables with an absolute correlation above 0.6, keeping the strongest per cluster, and stepwise multivariate selection at a 1% significance level with business review; the nine final drivers all have the expected sign: behavioural score (negative), maximum arrears in the last 12 months (positive), indexed LTV (positive), payment shock at rate reset (positive), NHG (negative), loan-to-income at origination (positive), seasoning (spline), change in unemployment (positive) and change in house prices (negative). No protected attribute was a candidate variable, and the postcode was excluded from the candidate set following the proxy screening in section 7.5 of the RDS documentation. From 14 macroeconomic candidates, the year-on-year change in the unemployment rate (lag two quarters, coefficient 0.21 per percentage point, p < 0.001) and the year-on-year change in the house price index (lag one quarter, coefficient −0.018 per percentage point, p < 0.001) were retained; GDP growth was rejected for collinearity with unemployment and a wrong sign in the multivariate model, and the mortgage rate because it is captured by the loan-level payment shock. Out of sample on 2024–2025, the macro-conditioned model reduced the absolute error of the predicted annual default rate from 0.08 to 0.03 percentage points compared with the model without macro terms.

sections.heading: PD – lifetime term structure and prepayment
sections.text: The monthly default hazard h_d and prepayment hazard h_p are chained into a lifetime term structure with survival S(t) = Π(1 − h_d(k) − h_p(k)) and marginal PD(t) = S(t−1) × h_d(t), over the remaining contractual maturity of each loan part, which gives a point-in-time PD term structure over the expected life of each exposure. The prepayment hazard comes from a multinomial logit model for full redemption and partial prepayment with drivers refinancing incentive, remaining fixed-rate period, penalty-free headroom, seasoning and regional housing turnover, estimated on 2015–2026, which reflects expected prepayments in the measurement; the baseline annual prepayment rate for 2027 is 5.8% against 5.4% observed in 2026. The macroeconomic drivers are applied over the reasonable and supportable forecast period of three years (2027–2029); in 2030–2031 they revert linearly to their long-run averages over two years, after which hazards correspond to the long-run default rate of 0.63%, so that ECL for exposures with lives beyond the forecast horizon is estimated by a documented process. By construction of the survival formulation cumulative PD curves are monotonically non-decreasing and marginal PDs are non-negative, and the ECL engine verifies both conditions per loan part at each run.

sections.heading: LGD
sections.text: For performing loan parts LGD = P(cure) × LGD_cure + (1 − P(cure)) × LGL; P(cure) is a logistic model with drivers indexed LTV, NHG, arrears amount and, for Stage 3, time in default (average 63%), and LGD_cure is 1.2% (costs and interest loss). The loss given liquidation is the shortfall of the exposure over the collateral proceeds, being the indexed property value projected with the scenario house price path, less a forced-sale discount of 12.5%, sale costs of 3.0% plus EUR 4,500, discounted over a time to sale of 16 months, and for NHG loan parts the guarantee payment with a claim acceptance rate of 94%; foreclosure proceeds are included whether or not foreclosure is probable. Collateral values are indexed from the latest valuation to the reporting date and projected with the scenario-specific regional (COROP) house price paths of each macroeconomic scenario. The LGD is a best estimate without downturn adjustment, margin of conservatism or regulatory LGD floors, and recoveries and directly attributable costs are discounted at the effective interest rate of the loan part. Loan parts are written off when the property has been sold and there is no reasonable expectation of recovering the residual debt; recoveries after write-off (on average 6% of the residual debt) are included in realised LGD, consistent with this write-off policy. The average LGD of performing loan parts is 7.4% in the baseline scenario, 5.8% in the upside and 12.9% in the downside scenario.

sections.heading: EAD and expected life
sections.text: The EAD term structure follows the contractual repayment schedule per loan part and repayment type, reduced by expected partial prepayments and including accrued interest; binding offers are converted with a credit conversion factor of 78%, estimated on the drawdown of offers within their validity period in 2019–2026. The expected life equals the remaining contractual maturity (on average 21.6 years, maximum 30 years), and the ECL horizon never exceeds the maximum contractual period over which the Bank is exposed to credit risk. The portfolio contains no revolving facilities, so the behavioural measurement period of IFRS 9 paragraph 5.5.20 and FIN-STD-200 §8.3 does not apply. Prepayment is accounted for consistently in the lifetime PD (as competing risk) and in the EAD (as balance reduction), using the same prepayment module.

sections.heading: Forward-looking information – scenarios and weights
sections.text: ECL is computed under the baseline, upside and downside scenarios produced by Enterprise Stress Testing under ERM-STD-300; the baseline equals the scenario of the financial plan 2027–2029 approved by the Management Board on 8 December 2026, so that forward-looking information is consistent with budgets and capital planning. The Q4 2026 baseline assumes Dutch GDP growth of 1.3%, 1.5% and 1.6% in 2027–2029, unemployment of 3.9–4.1% and house price growth of 4.5%, 3.0% and 2.5%; the downside assumes a GDP contraction of 1.8% in 2027, unemployment peaking at 6.4% in 2028 and a cumulative house price fall of 15% over 2027–2028; the upside assumes GDP growth of 2.4%, unemployment of 3.5% and house price growth of 7.0% in 2027. For Q4 2026 the Group Impairment Committee set the weights at 50% baseline, 20% upside and 30% downside, with no scenario below 10%, based on the position of each scenario in the distribution of GDP outcomes from the stochastic simulation of Enterprise Stress Testing, supplemented by the Committee's view on downside risks.

sections.heading: Forward-looking information – scenario ECL and non-linearity
sections.text: ECL is calculated separately under each scenario and then probability-weighted: at 31 December 2026 the modelled ECL is EUR 70.9 million under 100% baseline, EUR 61.2 million under 100% upside and EUR 100.3 million under 100% downside, and the weighted ECL is EUR 77.8 million, so the non-linearity effect of EUR 6.9 million is reported quarterly to the Group Impairment Committee. The average 12-month PD of performing loan parts is 0.43% in the baseline, 0.36% in the upside and 0.71% in the downside scenario, and the average performing LGD is 7.4%, 5.8% and 12.9%, which demonstrates how the ECL components change with the scenarios. Every loan part has a strictly positive PD and LGD in each scenario, so that the estimate reflects both the possibility that a credit loss occurs and the possibility that none occurs. Between 31 December 2025 and 31 December 2026 house prices rose by 8.2% and unemployment remained at 3.8–3.9%, and the modelled ECL decreased from EUR 84.1 million to EUR 77.8 million, mainly through lower LGDs, which is directionally consistent with the observable data. The scenario weights, the ECL under 100% of each scenario and a qualitative description of how forward-looking information is incorporated are provided to Finance for the IFRS 7 disclosures in the annual report.

sections.heading: ECL calculation, discounting and modifications
sections.text: Expected cash shortfalls are discounted to the reporting date, not to the expected default date, using the effective interest rate of the loan part determined at initial recognition; for variable-rate loan parts (3.4% of the balance) the current effective interest rate is used. The resulting estimate is unbiased and probability-weighted, reflects a range of outcomes and the time value of money and uses reasonable and supportable information available without undue cost or effort, and contains no margins of conservatism, downturn components or regulatory floors. The ECL engine calculates the monthly terms per loan part and scenario up to the remaining maturity, aggregates them to 12-month ECL (first 12 months) and lifetime ECL, and applies the stage from the staging module. Results are reported per loan part to the finance subledger and aggregated by stage, product, NHG status and LTV band for management reporting. For modifications that do not result in derecognition, Finance recalculates the gross carrying amount as the present value of the modified contractual cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate and recognises a modification gain or loss in profit or loss, and the ECL engine uses the recalculated gross carrying amount. A modification leads to derecognition when the present value of the modified cash flows differs by more than 10% from that of the original cash flows or on qualitative grounds such as a change of borrower; a new loan recognised after derecognition of a credit-impaired loan is identified as POCI. Interest rate resets at the end of a fixed-rate period are contractual repricings and not modifications. In 2026, 1,840 forbearance measures were granted, with modification losses of EUR 0.9 million.

sections.heading: Stage 3 and purchased or originated credit-impaired assets
sections.text: Stage 3 comprises the loan parts of obligors in default under CR-STD-110, whose triggers capture the observable events of the IFRS 9 definition of a credit-impaired asset, namely significant financial difficulty of the borrower, a breach of contract such as more than 90 days past due, distressed concessions and probable bankruptcy, including the combined effect of several events through the case-by-case UTP assessment. For Stage 3 obligors with a total exposure of EUR 1 million or more (23 obligors, EUR 31 million), the workout function measures ECL individually as the difference between the gross carrying amount and the present value of probability-weighted estimated cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate; all other Stage 3 loan parts use the LGD module with time-in-default dependent LGD. Fourteen loan parts (EUR 3.1 million) are purchased or originated credit-impaired, arising from the derecognition of forborne loans; for these the allowance equals only the cumulative change in lifetime ECL since initial recognition, without staging.

sections.heading: Reconciliation with IRB definitions and parameters
sections.text: Key terms are defined consistently with credit risk management and the IRB approach: default follows CR-STD-110, loss is the economic loss including directly attributable costs, and cure follows the exit from default; the differences with the IRB parameters (point-in-time instead of long-run and downturn calibration, discounting at the effective interest rate instead of the IRB discount rate, lifetime instead of 12-month horizon) and their rationale were approved by the Group Impairment Committee on 17 October 2024 as part of the approval of version 3.0. The IRB LGD model for residential mortgages is not reused; applying its downturn LGD including margin of conservatism would raise the average performing LGD from 7.4% to 14.8% and the modelled ECL at 31 December 2026 by EUR 41 million, which quantifies the effect of the IFRS 9-specific design choices. Both models use the same cure definition and the same forced-sale data, so that differences between the two parameters are limited to the framework-driven design choices listed above.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: The intercept of the hazard model is calibrated so that the predicted 12-month default rate over 2024–2026 equals the observed default rate of 0.40% adjusted to current conditions through the macroeconomic terms; the long-run average default rate is not used as the calibration target. After calibration the predicted 12-month default rate for 2026 is 0.43% against an observed 0.41%. For performance testing and monitoring, loan parts are grouped into ten PD bands (P01–P10, from below 0.05% to above 5%), which are not used for staging or measurement. The prepayment model is calibrated to the observed 2024–2026 prepayment rates, and the cure model and the forced-sale discount to 2022–2026 workouts and sales, while the loss given liquidation parameters are reviewed annually against the most recent sales.

The data deficiencies of the RDS documentation are treated as described in its section 6.2 and in the limitations log in chapter 8.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power and stability
sections.text: Discriminatory power of the 12-month hazard model was tested on the development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples with thresholds consistent with MV-HB-003: the Gini coefficient is 0.83 on development, 0.82 on out-of-sample and 0.81 on out-of-time data (95% DeLong interval 0.79–0.83), well above the red threshold of 0.50 for retail behavioural PD. The Gini of the previous model version 3.1 on the same out-of-time sample is 0.80. The ordering of default rates across the ten PD bands is monotonic on all three samples. Stability was tested by the PSI of the score and drivers between the development sample and the out-of-time sample (score 0.05, drivers 0.01–0.11) and by re-estimating the model on rolling five-year windows, in which all coefficients keep their sign and remain within two standard errors of the full-sample estimate. The stage distribution was stable over the last eight quarters, with a Stage 2 share between 6.8% and 7.6% of exposure. The prepayment model is stable except for 2022, when the refinancing incentive turned negative; the model captures this through the incentive driver.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and performance by segment
sections.text: Calibration accuracy was tested on the out-of-time sample with the Jeffreys test applied two-sided, as required for unbiased IFRS 9 estimates: at portfolio level the predicted default rate (0.44%) is not significantly different from the observed rate (0.42%, p = 0.41), and per PD band nine bands are green and band P07 shows significant overestimation (p = 0.03, amber). The overestimation in P07 was analysed and attributed to loans with a payment shock indicator whose rate reset occurred at lower market rates than assumed, and is recorded in the limitations log as L-09 with recalibration of the payment shock variable planned for version 4.0. Performance was tested for the whole model and for each material segment (NHG and non-NHG, annuity, linear, interest-only and savings-linked products, LTV bands and PD bands): Gini ranges from 0.74 (interest-only) to 0.84 (annuity). The only metric outside its threshold is the calibration of the interest-only segment on the out-of-time sample (observed 0.52% against predicted 0.44%, amber), analysed as caused by refinancing risk at maturity that is not captured by the drivers, recorded as limitation L-01 and addressed by overlay OVL-M-01 and the planned model change to version 4.0. The LGD model performs within tolerance for NHG and non-NHG loans (section 7.7).

sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger model
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model, the model is compared with a challenger model, the TTC-to-PIT conversion of the IRB PD (approach B of section 4.1), which is run quarterly in parallel. On the out-of-time sample the challenger has a Gini of 0.74 against 0.81 and a larger calibration error (0.11 against 0.02 percentage points), and at 31 December 2026 it produces a modelled ECL of EUR 82.4 million against EUR 77.8 million; the difference is explained by the higher lifetime PDs of the challenger for seasoned annuity loans, whose static lifetime curve does not reflect their amortisation, so the challenger does not outperform the model on any material metric. The ECL coverage ratio of 15 basis points is within the range of 9–18 basis points disclosed by four other Dutch mortgage lenders for 2026, which serves as an external benchmark.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and input data and are reported against the modelled ECL of EUR 77.8 million at 31 December 2026: SICR thresholds 2.0/0.20 (+EUR 4.1 million) and 2.5/0.50 (−EUR 2.9 million); forced-sale discount ±5 percentage points (±EUR 6.2 million); prepayment rate ±2 percentage points (∓EUR 1.8 million); calibration window 2023–2025 instead of 2024–2026 (+EUR 1.1 million); reversion period of one or three years (−EUR 0.4 million / +EUR 0.5 million); exclusion of the imputed valuations (+EUR 0.3 million); and 100% weight on each scenario (section 4.6.2). The material expert judgements (EJ-MDD-02 reversion period, EJ-MDD-04 NHG claim acceptance rate and EJ-MDD-05 forced-sale discount floor) are quantified by these sensitivities, which test reasonable alternative judgements. No sensitivity changes the ECL by more than 10%, and none changes the stage of more than 2% of the exposure except the SICR threshold variants.

sections.heading: Back-testing of staging, PD, LGD and CCF
sections.text: Back-testing is performed annually: the 12-month PIT PD per PD band against observed default rates (section 7.2), LGD on closed workouts, the conversion factor of binding offers, and the stage allocation, including the share of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default and the frequency of stage reversals. For 2026 the share of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default is 71% (2025: 68%), stage reversals from Stage 2 to Stage 1 within three months affect 11.4% of transfers, the predicted LGD on 2025–2026 closed workouts is 9.6% against a realised 8.9%, and the predicted conversion of offers is 78% against 81% observed. Internally established performance standards are defined for each back-testing metric in chapter 10, and a significant breach leads to remedial action up to recalibration or redevelopment.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: All material assumptions on data, driver–target relationships, their stability and the intended use have been identified and assessed for plausibility: (A1) the relationship between defaults, prepayments and macroeconomic conditions observed in 2012–2026 continues to hold; (A2) regional house price paths from the scenario models are unbiased; (A3) the forced-sale discount and sale costs remain stable; (A4) mortgages are not extended beyond their contractual maturity; (A5) NHG claims are honoured at the observed acceptance rate; (A6) the proxy origination PD for pre-2018 loans is representative. A1 and A2 are supported by the out-of-time and macro back-testing results, A3 and A5 are reviewed annually against realised sales and claims, A4 follows from the contractual terms and A6 is supported by the comparison in section 4.2.5. The assumptions are reviewed at each annual model review.

sections.heading: Reporting, escalation and annual review
sections.text: Monitoring results are reported to the model owner, Model Risk Management, Model Validation and Credit Risk Management. Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive quarters, is notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, followed within 60 calendar days by a root cause analysis and an action plan proposing no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use. In line with FIN-STD-200 §12.3 a red outcome leads to an MRC-approved remediation plan within three months and an assessment of the need for a temporary overlay. The annual model review by the model owner covers monitoring results, portfolio and environment changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and overlays, and code-documentation consistency, and concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose; it is signed off by the model owner and submitted to MRM (for 2026: report EVD-07-MON).

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: Every expert judgement applied in the development and application of the model is recorded in the expert judgement log EJL-MDL-07, stored with the model documentation, with its type, lifecycle stage and affected data, segment or parameter; judgements in data treatment are also referenced in the RDS documentation. Each entry records the rationale, the evidence relied on and the alternatives considered and rejected, and the quantified impact on the ECL or the reason why quantification is not possible. The log contains eight active entries: EJ-RDS-01 (COVID-19 payment holiday treatment), EJ-RDS-02 (product code mapping), EJ-MDD-01 (single PD model with segment drivers), EJ-MDD-02 (two-year reversion period), EJ-MDD-03 (rejection of GDP as driver), EJ-MDD-04 (NHG claim acceptance rate), EJ-MDD-05 (forced-sale discount floor of 10%) and EJ-OVL-01 (quantification of overlay OVL-M-01); each is described in this chapter or in the overlay memo with its log reference.
